Conditional LATE from supplied nuisance predictions

Source: vignettes/conditional-late.Rmd
conditional-late.Rmd

clate_dnn() estimates conditional effects among compliers using a binary instrument A, binary treatment D and supplied nuisance predictions. The paper defines the causal target and identifying assumptions. Reporting covariates can be a subset of the controls used to obtain the nuisance predictions.

Exactly identical reporting-covariate rows share their block’s average weight in both the reduced form and first stage, even when their outcomes or nuisance predictions differ. Each deletion removes the actual row and redistributes its remaining block’s n-1 weight-table mass over the survivors. This is a ratio of two weighted signal averages, not an average of individual ratios. The package warns that the block-averaging modification is outside the paper’s theory. See the weight guide.

Fit from a data frame

This synthetic example uses oracle predictions. The five nuisance vectors are the instrument propensity and the outcome/treatment means in each instrument arm. Arm indices refer to the instrument, not treatment.

demo <- clate_demo_data(n = 120, seed = 20261017, heterogeneous = TRUE)
d <- demo$data
targets <- rbind(c(.25, .25), c(.5, .5), c(.75, .75))
fit <- clate_dnn(
  data = d, x_cols = c("X1", "X2"), X0 = targets,
  y_col = "Y", d_col = "D", a_col = "A", e_col = "e_oracle",
  m_y0_col = "m_y0_oracle", m_y1_col = "m_y1_oracle",
  m_d0_col = "m_d0_oracle", m_d1_col = "m_d1_oracle",
  training = "oracle", row_ids = d$row_id, tuning_mode = "grid",
  return = c("W", "dx")
)
summary(fit)$coefficients
#>             estimate std.error  statistic   p.value    conf.low conf.high
#> target_1 -0.09891197 0.1918865 -0.5154713 0.6062237 -0.47500253 0.2771786
#> target_2  0.20115037 0.1265871  1.5890271 0.1120543 -0.04695583 0.4492566
#> target_3  0.04455010 0.1014209  0.4392594 0.6604736 -0.15423127 0.2433315

The default fit is retained while the grid compares alternative orders; it does not select a preferred candidate. training records provenance and fits no models. In an application, merge external predictions onto the observations using stable IDs before fitting. IDs supplied to the estimator cannot detect a prediction vector that was independently reordered.

For matrix inputs, pass the same vectors directly. Here the order is held at the fitted default so the two calls can be compared:

X <- as.matrix(d[c("X1", "X2")])
fit_matrix <- clate_dnn(
  X = X, X0 = targets, Y = d$Y, D = d$D, A = d$A,
  e = d$e_oracle, m_y0 = d$m_y0_oracle, m_y1 = d$m_y1_oracle,
  m_d0 = d$m_d0_oracle, m_d1 = d$m_d1_oracle,
  s = fit$meta$s, se = FALSE
)
data.frame(data_frame = coef(fit), matrix = coef(fit_matrix))
#>           data_frame      matrix
#> target_1 -0.09891197 -0.09891197
#> target_2  0.20115037  0.20115037
#> target_3  0.04455010  0.04455010

Tibbles use the data-frame interface. All reporting covariates and prediction vectors must be finite and aligned. Raw instrument propensities and treatment predictions must lie in [0,1]. Propensities are clipped with clip = 1e-8 by default; clipping does not create overlap.

For a genuinely one-sided design, one_sided = TRUE permits omission of m_d0; observed treatment must satisfy D <= A. The observed check cannot establish the structural restriction. See ?clate_dnn for its input rules.

Read the first stage alongside the effect 

fit$components
#>        numerator denominator
#> [1,] -0.03687344   0.3727905
#> [2,]  0.10219813   0.5080683
#> [3,]  0.03033088   0.6808264
diagnostic <- as.data.frame(diagnostics(fit))
diagnostic[, c("target_id", "denominator", "denominator_se",
               "ratio_status", "wald_available")]
#>          target_id denominator denominator_se ratio_status wald_available
#> target_1  target_1   0.3727905      0.2335520           ok           TRUE
#> target_2  target_2   0.5080683      0.2577646           ok           TRUE
#> target_3  target_3   0.6808264      0.1880182           ok           TRUE

The numerator is the adjusted reduced form and the denominator is the adjusted first stage. Their paired covariance enters ratio uncertainty. vcov(fit) returns marginal ratio covariance matrices, one per profile; it does not supply cross-profile covariance. These are estimator-scale variances and must not be divided by effective sample size again.

An exactly zero first stage leaves the ratio undefined; finite negative first stages retain a signed ratio. A finite estimate can have unavailable Wald bounds. Inspect statuses and components before interpreting the output. Weak local first stages can make Wald intervals unreliable. The inference guide explains these fields, covariance scales and the separate experimental confidence-set helper.

Supply two signals directly

If another workflow constructs the augmented signals, localize their means with affine_ratio_dnn(). The package’s signal constructor gives the same inputs explicitly:

signals <- iv_augmented_signals(
  Y = d$Y, D = d$D, A = d$A, e = d$e_oracle,
  m_y0 = d$m_y0_oracle, m_y1 = d$m_y1_oracle,
  m_d0 = d$m_d0_oracle, m_d1 = d$m_d1_oracle
)
ratio <- affine_ratio_dnn(
  X = X, X0 = targets,
  numerator = signals$phi_y, denominator = signals$phi_d,
  s = fit$meta$s
)
data.frame(clate = coef(fit), paired_signals = coef(ratio))
#>                clate paired_signals
#> target_1 -0.09891197    -0.09891197
#> target_2  0.20115037     0.20115037
#> target_3  0.04455010     0.04455010

Both components use common weights. Average the two signals before dividing; observation-level signal ratios define a different statistic. Generic paired signals carry no instrument record for overlap plots. Use the nuisance-based CLATE fit when those diagnostics are needed.

Plot and reuse the fit

With ggplot2 installed:

plot(fit, style = "forest")

plot_overlap(fit, type = "mass")

Weight/kernel and influence views also use the shared plotting API. Keep "W" for weight panels and "dx" for distance-based kernels. See Visualising fits for plot controls.

Extract one grid candidate or evaluate a new profile using retained signals:

candidate <- candidate_fit(fit, 1L)
coef(candidate)
#>    target_1    target_2    target_3 
#> -0.07448888  0.17443055  0.09002873
predict(fit, x0 = c(.6, .4), interval = "confidence")
#>              fit        lwr       upr
#> [1,] -0.09169375 -0.5886832 0.4052957

Neither operation refits nuisance learners. Saved fits contain observation-level numeric values and inherit the data’s sharing restrictions. predict() relocalizes those frozen signals; it does not predict outcomes for new people. For order controls, see Kernel-order tuning. For result fields, see Notation and conventions.
